blogPosts.title: Why Feature Stores Are the Backbone of Production ML
blogPosts.excerpt: Training-serving skew is the default, not the exception — here is how to close the gap.
blogPosts.author: James Mwangi
blogPosts.content:
Most models fail in production not because the model is wrong, but because the features feeding it drift silently between training and serving. A feature store closes that gap by giving every model — batch or real-time — one governed source of truth.

Training-serving skew is the default, not the exception

Without a shared registry, teams recompute the same features twice: once offline in a notebook, once online in a service. The two implementations drift the moment either one changes.

What good looks like

A feature store gives point-in-time correctness for training sets, low-latency lookups for inference, and lineage so risk and compliance teams can trace any prediction back to its inputs.

blogPosts.title: LLM Agents in Regulated Environments
blogPosts.excerpt: What compliance teams need to know before shipping an automation agent.
blogPosts.author: Amara Ochieng
blogPosts.content:
An automation agent that can read a claim, call three internal systems and make a decision is a very different animal from a chatbot. In a regulated environment, every one of those actions needs to be attributable, reversible and explainable after the fact.

Give the agent a narrower mandate than the model can handle

The model's raw capability is not the constraint — the audit trail is. We scope agents to a fixed set of tool calls with typed inputs and outputs, so every action the agent takes is a structured, loggable event rather than free-form text.

Human-in-the-loop is a design decision, not a fallback

Decide up front which decision classes require sign-off, and build the review queue as a first-class part of the system rather than an afterthought bolted on once an auditor asks for one.

blogPosts.title: Real-Time Risk Scoring at Scale
blogPosts.excerpt: Architecture patterns for sub-100ms decisioning under regulatory load.
blogPosts.author: David Otieno
blogPosts.content:
A credit or fraud decision that takes 300ms feels instant to a person and glacial to a payment rail. Getting under 100ms end-to-end means treating the scoring path as a hard real-time system, not a web request with a model attached.

Keep the hot path free of anything that can block

Feature lookups happen from an in-memory or sub-millisecond store, never from the same transactional database that serves the rest of the platform. Anything that can be computed ahead of time — aggregates, embeddings, risk tiers — is precomputed and cached.

Design for the regulator's replay, not just the customer's request

Every scored transaction is logged with the exact feature values and model version used, so a disputed decision can be reconstructed exactly as it happened months later.

blogPosts.title: From Notebook to Production: An MLOps Maturity Model
blogPosts.excerpt: A five-stage framework for auditing your model deployment pipeline.
blogPosts.author: Sofia Ngugi
blogPosts.content:
Most teams don't lack machine learning talent — they lack a repeatable path from a working notebook to a model that ships, retrains and gets retired safely. We use a five-stage maturity model to diagnose exactly where a pipeline breaks down.

Stages 1–3: notebook, script, pipeline

Stage one is a data scientist's notebook. Stage two wraps that logic in a versioned script anyone can rerun. Stage three orchestrates it as a scheduled, monitored pipeline with data validation at every step.

Stages 4–5: continuous training, full observability

Stage four retrains automatically against fresh data and gates promotion behind offline evaluation. Stage five adds production observability — drift detection, shadow deployments and automatic rollback — so a regression is caught before it reaches a customer.

blogPosts.title: Algorithmic Trading Infrastructure: Latency, Risk, Resilience
blogPosts.excerpt: Design tradeoffs behind execution systems that cannot go down.
blogPosts.author: Lindiwe Banda
blogPosts.content:
An execution system has three competing priorities — speed, correctness and uptime — and every architectural decision trades one against another. The systems that survive a bad day are the ones that made that tradeoff deliberately.

Latency budgets belong on a whiteboard, not in a retro

We assign an explicit microsecond budget to every hop — market data ingestion, signal generation, risk checks, order routing — and treat any component that exceeds its budget as a defect, not an optimization opportunity for later.

Risk checks are not the thing that slows you down

Pre-trade risk limits run in the same process as the execution logic, compiled against the same market state, so safety and speed stop being in tension with each other.

blogPosts.title: Designing Dashboards Executives Actually Use
blogPosts.excerpt: Decision intelligence beats vanity metrics — a framework for both.
blogPosts.author: Paula Carmen
blogPosts.content:
Most executive dashboards get opened once, admired, and never touched again. The ones that survive share one trait: every number on the screen is tied to a decision someone actually has to make that week.

Start from the decision, not the data warehouse

Before building a single chart, we write down the three decisions the dashboard needs to inform and work backward to the minimum set of metrics that move those decisions.

Vanity metrics crowd out decision intelligence

A dashboard with forty tiles trains people to stop looking. We'd rather ship four numbers an executive can defend in a board meeting than forty they can't explain.
